summary: This RFC specifies using TLS over TCP as a transport for RADIUS, giving encryption and enabling dynamic trust relationships between RADIUS servers. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RADIUS is the protocol many networks use to check who a user is when they connect. The old version sends its messages unprotected over UDP. This memo sends RADIUS inside a TLS tunnel over TCP instead, so the traffic is encrypted and the two ends prove who they are with certificates. It is an experiment, not yet a full Internet Standard.

subtitle: Running RADIUS authentication over TLS on TCP so roaming traffic is encrypted and peers check certificates instead of shared secrets.

tldr.problem: Classic RADIUS relies on the unreliable UDP transport and protects packets with MD5, which is known to be weak, and it identifies peers by IP address and a shared secret, which does not scale across administrative domains.
tldr.mechanism: This profile runs RADIUS over TCP, then immediately wraps the connection in TLS with mutual certificate authentication, so the whole RADIUS payload travels inside an encrypted tunnel.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental RFC, one of several attempts to fix RADIUS cryptography; it was later updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9765.

today: RADIUS over TLS is an Experimental RFC published in May 2012 and has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9765. The RFC itself says it does not fulfil every recommendation for a AAA transport profile, because being based on TCP it does not prevent head-of-line blocking, and that certificate verification and key management would need refinement before any move to Standards Track.

sections.title: Encrypting RADIUS with TLS
sections.content:
RADIUS is a widely deployed authentication and authorization protocol, with a companion accounting specification that together deliver a full Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) solution. It has known shortcomings: it depends on the unreliable UDP transport and much of its packet payload is not secured, and its protection rests on the MD5 algorithm, which has been shown to be insecure.

RADIUS over TLS wraps the entire RADIUS packet payload in a TLS stream and so reduces the risk from attacks on MD5. It matters most in roaming environments, where RADIUS packets cross different administrative domains and untrusted, potentially hostile networks. The example named in the RFC is the worldwide roaming environment eduroam. Because the new transport replaces IP addresses and shared MD5 secrets used to identify peers, it also permits more contemporary trust models, such as checking a certificate's issuer and other properties.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS checks identities for network access, but its older form sends much of the information unprotected and relies on a weak old algorithm. Wrapping RADIUS in TLS protects the whole message, which especially matters when the traffic crosses networks run by different organizations.

sections.title: TCP Port and TLS Negotiation
sections.content:
The default destination port for RADIUS over TLS is TCP port 2083, with no separate ports for authentication, accounting and dynamic authorization changes; the source port is arbitrary. There is no negotiation of TLS within an already established connection: servers and clients must be preconfigured to use RADIUS over TLS for a given endpoint.

A node first establishes a TCP connection. If the connection fails, it retries continuously with exponentially growing intervals, and if several servers are defined it may try them in parallel for quick failover. After the TCP handshake it immediately negotiates TLS, with these restrictions: support for TLS version 1.1 or later is required and earlier versions must not be negotiated; certificate-based mutual authentication is required and must be negotiated; a ciphersuite giving both confidentiality and integrity is required, because otherwise the entire payload, including user passwords, could be recovered by third parties. Compression is optional, TLS-PSK mutual authentication is optional, and implementations must at minimum support TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA and should also support TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA and TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection is set up in two steps: first an ordinary reliable connection on port 2083, then an encrypted TLS session on top of it, using a recent version of TLS and a cipher that both hides and protects the data. Both ends have to be configured for this; nothing is negotiated informally.

sections.title: How Peers Prove Who They Are
sections.content:
Peer authentication works in one of three models. The mandatory model uses X.509 certificates with PKIX trust models: implementations must allow a list of trusted certification authorities for incoming connections, certificate validation must follow the verification rules in RFC 5280, and peer validation always checks whether the expected DNS name or IP address matches the presented certificate, with subjectAltName taking precedence over the common name. Two optional models exist: certificates identified by the fingerprint of the DER-encoded certificate, and TLS pre-shared keys.

RADIUS over TLS also changes how a client is identified. In classic RADIUS, clients are identified by IP address, which forces clients sharing an address to share a secret. Here, a TLS-PSK client is identified by its TLS identifier; a client using fingerprints is identified by the certificate fingerprint; and a client using PKIX is identified by the pair of the certificate serial number and the issuer. Being identified does not mean the server must accept the client: if the issuer is not in a trusted set, the server may decline the transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side proves who it is using a certificate, checked against a list of trusted authorities and against the name it expected. Choosing a fingerprint or a pre-shared key is also allowed. This replaces the old scheme where peers were trusted only by their address and a shared password.

sections.title: Sending RADIUS Datagrams
sections.content:
Clients send the same packet types they would over UDP, such as Access-Request, Accounting-Request, Status-Server, Disconnect-ACK and Disconnect-NAK, and receive replies such as Access-Accept, Accounting-Response and Disconnect-Request. Servers send Access-Challenge, Access-Accept, Access-Reject, Accounting-Response and Disconnect-Request, and receive Access-Request, Accounting-Request, Status-Server and Disconnect-ACK.

Because a single TCP port carries all packet types, a server must signal which types it supports. When an unwanted CoA-Request or Disconnect-Request arrives, the server responds with a CoA-NAK or Disconnect-NAK, and the NAK should carry an Error-Cause attribute with the value 406, Unsupported Extension. When an unwanted Accounting-Request arrives, the server should reply with an Accounting-Response carrying the same Error-Cause value, and a client receiving it should log the error and stop sending accounting requests.

Two consequences of using a stream are notable. Packet boundaries can no longer be found from the datagram size, so a receiver works out where a packet ends from its Length field, and the sender must ensure that field is correct. And because TLS supplies integrity and encryption, no real RADIUS shared secret is needed, so the obsolete MD5 computations use the fixed string "radsec", which removes a source of misconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are the same as before, but they now travel inside one stream. Since one port carries everything, the server has to say what it supports and answer unwanted requests with a refusal. The old shared password is replaced by the fixed word radsec because TLS already does the protecting.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Compatibility
sections.content:
Setting up a TLS tunnel costs far more than sending mostly unencrypted UDP datagrams, so clients can more easily create high load and a malicious client can mount a denial-of-service attack more easily. Ciphersuites that provide only integrity and no encryption are forbidden, since with the shared secret fixed to "radsec" a failure to encrypt would expose the whole payload, including passwords, to intermediate nodes. Being based on TCP also exposes the known attacks that slow down or prevent a connection from being established, though these normally cause only minor delay. One exception is a bidding-down attack during migration: if a peer is configured for both RADIUS over TLS and RADIUS over UDP as a failover, an adversary who prevents the TLS session can reduce protection to MD5, so the weaker UDP transport should be disabled once TLS works.

The RFC stresses that encryption is between RADIUS peers only. With proxies in the path, intermediate proxies can still inspect individual RADIUS packets, so end-to-end encryption is not provided; where proxies are untrusted, other mechanisms such as EAP methods that use TLS should protect passwords. When certificate fingerprints identify peers, any two certificates with the same hash are treated as the same client, so the hash function must be uncompromised. RADIUS over TLS is not backward or cross compatible with the other transports; an implementation that serves several transports is called a multi-stack implementation, and two transports on one device must be considered separate RADIUS server entities.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption costs more work than plain sending, which makes overload and attack easier. It also protects each leg of the journey, not the whole path, so proxies still see the content. During a changeover, an attacker could push traffic back to the weaker old way, so the old path should be switched off once the new one works.
